text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
author: Epictetus
context: Stoic philosopher, Enchiridion (c. 125 AD, in translation). The core idea behind modern cognitive therapy.

text: The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven.
author: John Milton
context: From Paradise Lost (1667). A 350-year-old take on how your perspective shapes your experience.

text: Nothing in life is as important as you think it is, while you are thinking about it.
author: Daniel Kahneman
context: Nobel-winning psychologist describing the focusing illusion in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).

text: Price is what you pay. Value is what you get.
author: Warren Buffett
context: From his 2008 Berkshire Hathaway letter, crediting mentor Ben Graham. Cheap and good value aren't the same.

text: Beware of little expenses; a small leak will sink a great ship.
author: Benjamin Franklin
context: From The Way to Wealth (1758). Subscriptions and daily coffees were not yet invented, but the math was.

text: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
author: Seneca
context: Roman Stoic, Letters to Lucilius (c. 65 AD, in translation). Wealth as a gap between what you have and want.

text: Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
author: George Santayana
context: Philosopher, The Life of Reason (1905). Often misquoted, but this is the original wording in English.

text: Veni, vidi, vici. (I came, I saw, I conquered.)
author: Julius Caesar
context: Caesar's famously brief message after a lightning win at Zela in 47 BC, per Plutarch and Suetonius.

text: The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.
author: Franklin D. Roosevelt
context: First inaugural address, 1933, as the US sat deep in the Great Depression and bank panics.

text: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.
author: Isaac Newton
context: Letter to Robert Hooke, 1675/76. Science as a relay race, not a solo sprint.

text: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.
author: Richard Feynman
context: Caltech commencement speech "Cargo Cult Science" (1974), on honesty in research.

text: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.
author: Carl Sagan
context: Popularized by Sagan in his TV series Cosmos (1980). A handy filter for anything you read online.

text: A planet is the cradle of mind, but one cannot live in a cradle forever.
author: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky
context: Russian rocketry pioneer, in a 1911 letter (in translation). He worked out rocket math decades before spaceflight.

text: Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us.
author: Carl Sagan
context: From Pale Blue Dot (1994), about Voyager 1's photo of Earth from about 6 billion km away.

text: We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.
author: John F. Kennedy
context: Speech at Rice University, 1962. Apollo 11 landed less than seven years later.

text: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
author: Benjamin Franklin
context: From a 1735 letter Franklin wrote urging Philadelphians to prevent fires. It applies just as well to your body.

text: Sleep is that golden chain that ties health and our bodies together.
author: Thomas Dekker
context: English playwright, The Gull's Hornbook (1609). Sleep science has only strengthened his point.

text: Those who think they have not time for bodily exercise will sooner or later have to find time for illness.
author: Edward Stanley, 15th Earl of Derby
context: From an 1873 address at Liverpool College. Still the best argument against "too busy to work out."

text: How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.
author: Annie Dillard
context: Pulitzer-winning author, The Writing Life (1989). Your calendar is your biography in progress.

text: I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.
author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
context: From a 1954 speech, quoting a former college president. It later inspired the Eisenhower Matrix.

text: The best is the enemy of the good.
author: Voltaire
context: French writer who popularized an Italian proverb in the 1760s-70s. The classic case for shipping over polishing.

text: Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
author: Arthur C. Clarke
context: The third of "Clarke's three laws," from Profiles of the Future (1973 edition).

text: The best way to predict the future is to invent it.
author: Alan Kay
context: Computer scientist at Xerox PARC, 1971. His team helped invent the modern graphical interface.

text: The Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves.
author: Ada Lovelace
context: From her 1843 notes on Babbage's machine, linking punched-card looms to computing.
